 By Teri Dreher PUBLISHED: November 20, 2026 at 12:16 PM CST | UPDATED: November 20, 2026 at 12:23 PM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Fun fact: Thanksgiving has its roots in national turmoil. Some things never change, do they?
 During the Civil War, a magazine editor named Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for a national Thanksgiving Day to promote unity. She won the support of President Lincoln, and on Oct. 3, 1863, he proclaimed a national day of thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday in November.
 Then, just after the attacks on Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, brought the U.S. into World War II, Congress passed a joint resolution officially designating Thanksgiving as a federal holiday and setting the date as the fourth Thursday in November. President Roosevelt signed it on Dec. 26, 1941.
 What does all of this have to do with Thanksgiving 2026? It’s easy to put holidays on autopilot and forget why we celebrate them, so this year let’s all take a deep breath and put some extra thought into how we observe our annual day of thanksgiving. Healthy habits — emotional as well as physical — can make the holiday, and all the forthcoming holidays, brighter for you and your loved ones. Here are some ideas.
 Practice kindness.
 Practicing kindness is a wonderful way to not only have a positive impact on the world but also to improve our own well-being. It has been shown to increase self-esteem, empathy and compassion, and improve mood. It can even decrease blood pressure and cortisol, a hormone directly correlated with stress. Kindness can also boost serotonin and dopamine, neurotransmitters in the brain that are associated with feelings of satisfaction, well-being and pleasure.
 Express gratitude.
 The simple process of saying thanks to someone in your life or writing down what you’re thankful for can give you a more positive attitude about life, lessen depression and anxiety and even improve sleep.
 A study conducted by Joel Wong at Indiana University in 2017 found that college students who reported poor mental health felt better when they wrote gratitude letters — whether or not they actually sent the letters.
 “This suggests that gratitude writing can be beneficial not just for healthy, well-adjusted individuals, but also for those who struggle with mental health concerns,” wrote Wong, a professor of counseling and counseling psychology who is continuing to study “gratitude interventions.”
 Encourage sobriety.
 The more researchers learn about alcohol, the less attractive it is. Increasingly, research is finding that the risks of even moderate alcohol intake outweigh its benefits. Alcohol consumption is a risk factor for several types of cancer, including breast, colorectal and oral cavity cancers. According to the National Cancer Institute , moderate drinkers have a 1.23-fold higher risk of alcohol-related cancers.
 Especially if a loved one is struggling with substance use disorder (SUD), try to organize activities that don’t revolve around alcohol, such as a touch football game, a walk around the block or watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade together.
 Enjoy your favorite Thanksgiving dishes.
 The typical Thanksgiving day food intake, including pre-meal grazing and dessert, is around 3,300 calories, according to the Calorie Control Council . That’s enough for two days!
 But research has found that passing on your favorites may not be a great idea because it may lead to overeating in subsequent days.
 “Don’t restrict yourself of your favorite foods on the Thanksgiving table — and certainly don’t feel guilty,” says Jen Haugen, a registered dietitian. Instead, remember that Thanksgiving is just one day, and you can resume a more reasonable diet on Friday.
 Find a turkey trot!
 There’s nothing like a brisk 5K walk or run to get Thanksgiving off on the right foot, literally. To find turkey trots in your area, visit runguides.com and filter your search by location and month.
 I think what all of these suggestions have in common is mindfulness, the practice of being aware of the here and now. Rather than letting Thanksgiving slide by in a blur, savor the day and find something to be thankful for, however small.
 • Teri (Dreher) Frykenberg is a registered nurse and board-certified patient advocate. She is the author of several books on advocacy and founder of Nurse Advocate Entrepreneur , which equips medical professionals with the knowledge and skills to start their own advocacy businesses. Contact her at Teri@NurseAdvocateEntrepreneur.com.
